title: 4  Leiden exercises with PBMC3k
text:
4.9 Answering the conceptual questions
Work through these without rerunning any code; they are meant to be answered from what you have already produced above.
What mathematical object did Leiden actually receive? A neighbour graph built from 10 principal components, specifically its weighted adjacency structure. It never received the raw gene expression matrix, and UMAP had not even been computed at the point Leiden ran in Exercise 3.
Did Leiden operate on the expression matrix directly, or on UMAP? Neither. It operated on the neighbour graph, itself derived from PCA coordinates, which were in turn derived from a normalized and scaled subset of the expression matrix. UMAP, computed afterward in Exercise 4, is a two-dimensional summary used only for display.
What changed when the number of neighbours changed, holding resolution fixed? The graph itself changed: the edge count, and which cells counted as connected to which. Exercise 6 showed this moving the cluster count and the agreement with the baseline substantially, confirming that \(k\) is a property of the graph construction step, not of Leiden’s optimization.
What changed when only the resolution changed? Nothing about the graph changed. Only the threshold Leiden uses to decide whether a group of cells is sufficiently well connected to remain one community changed, exactly as Chapter 3 derived algebraically for CPM’s merge condition.
Why can the cluster numbers differ between R and Python even when the biological grouping is similar? Cluster labels are arbitrary integers assigned in whatever order the implementation happens to produce them. Seurat and Scanpy use different normalization defaults, different variable-gene selection formulas, and different underlying Leiden bindings, so exact cluster boundaries can differ in detail even when both recover recognizably the same broad populations, as they did throughout this chapter.
Why might a continuous biological trajectory be poorly summarized by a large number of Leiden clusters? Leiden always returns discrete, non-overlapping groups. If the underlying biology changes gradually, such as along a maturation or activation gradient, there is no natural break point for Leiden to find, and a high resolution will simply cut the continuum into arbitrary segments. Chapter 1’s comparison with Diffusion Maps discussed this limitation directly.
Which clusters appear robust across reasonable parameter choices? Based on the exercises above, the B-cell, monocyte, NK, and megakaryocyte populations appear as their own separated islands in UMAP space and persist as recognizable, marker-supported clusters across the resolution and neighbour-count sweeps. The finer subdivisions within the T-cell compartment are the least stable: they appear or disappear depending on resolution, shift under different neighbour counts, and are the primary source of disagreement across random seeds in Exercise 7.

title: 4  Leiden exercises with PBMC3k
text:
4.10 Diagnostics and practical advice
The exercises above touched resolution sensitivity, neighbour-count sensitivity, the number of principal components, edge weighting, and random seeds directly. A few more points are worth keeping in mind whenever you run this workflow on new data, even though the small size of PBMC3k does not illustrate all of them clearly.
Distance and similarity choice. Every graph in this course used Euclidean distance on PCA coordinates, the standard default in both Seurat and Scanpy. Other distances are sometimes used for other data types; whichever is chosen, \(\varepsilon\)-style radius arguments elsewhere in your analysis pipeline, and the general notion of what counts as “close,” change along with it.
Batch effects. If cells in your own data come from multiple samples, donors, or sequencing runs, technical differences between batches can dominate the neighbour graph, pulling cells together by batch of origin rather than by cell type. This course’s PBMC3k data comes from a single sample and does not illustrate this problem, but a real multi-sample analysis normally applies a batch-correction step before building the neighbour graph, not after. Leiden clusters whatever graph it is given, and it cannot distinguish a batch effect from real biological structure once both are baked into the graph.
Small clusters and rare populations. A biologically real but rare population, such as the 14-cell cluster found in Exercise 3, can look similar to an artifact of over-splitting a larger population. Marker-gene support, as in Exercise 4, and persistence across the resolution and neighbour-count sweeps of Exercises 5 and 6, are better evidence than cluster size alone. Neither is definitive proof on its own.
Disconnected graphs and isolated cells. A cell with no close neighbours under the chosen distance and \(k\) can end up in its own small component of the graph, or fail to connect meaningfully to any community. Leiden’s connectivity guarantee from Chapter 3 ensures the communities it returns are internally connected; it does not prevent a poorly connected input graph from producing a poorly supported partition in the first place.
Repeated runs and cluster stability. Exercise 7 showed real variation across random seeds even at fixed settings. Running Leiden more than once, at the settings you intend to use, and checking whether the broad structure persists, is a cheap way to catch a result that happens to be unusually sensitive to the specific random draw.
Marker genes and biological validation. A cluster is a statement about graph connectivity, not automatically a statement about cell identity. Connecting a cluster to a known biological label always requires independent evidence, ordinarily marker gene expression, exactly as Exercise 4 did.
None of this points to one universally correct resolution, one correct value of \(k\), or one correct number of principal components. It also does not mean the highest modularity or CPM score automatically identifies the biologically correct clustering, or that a silhouette score can be used as a universal stopping rule for a method that does not operate in a continuous coordinate space to begin with. A Leiden clustering is best interpreted together with the scientific question being asked, the marker evidence for each cluster, the stability of the result under reasonable parameter changes, and, where available, independent knowledge of the biology.

title: 4  Leiden exercises with PBMC3k
section: 4.11 What this chapter did not do
text:
4.11 What this chapter did not do
This chapter did not search for a single correct resolution, and it did not report a silhouette score or a modularity value as a selection rule. Both would have implied a false sense of a uniquely correct answer. What Chapter 3 established mathematically, and what this chapter has now shown directly on real data, is that a Leiden clustering is conditional on every choice that produced its input graph and every setting given to the algorithm itself. Reporting a clustering without reporting those choices leaves out exactly the information needed to judge it.

title: 1  Leiden clustering
text:
1.12 Refinement
Look again at the coarse community \(ABCDEF\) from Figure 1.9, and watch it get taken apart.







Figure 1.10: Refinement examines a coarse community’s internal structure. Starting from the coarse community ABCDEF, its internal structure is inspected, ABC and DEF are identified as internally well-connected pieces, and those pieces are kept separate when the next graph is built.




Figure 1.10 reads left to right. The first panel is the coarse community exactly as local moving left it, one single group. The second panel temporarily sets that grouping aside and looks only at the edges inside it. The third panel identifies \(\{A,B,C\}\) and \(\{D,E,F\}\) as two internally well-connected pieces, based on the strong triangle edges within each and the weak single edge between them. The fourth panel keeps those two pieces separate going forward.
This distinction matters and is easy to miss. Refinement does not simply mean splitting the final answer into smaller pieces at the end. It happens during the algorithm, before aggregation, and its output is used to build the next, smaller graph that the algorithm continues working on. The refined pieces are not yet the final clusters. They are the units that the next round of local moving is allowed to move as a whole.

title: 1  Leiden clustering
text:
1.13 Supernodes
Refinement produced two pieces, \(X = \{A,B,C\}\) and \(Y = \{D,E,F\}\). Aggregation turns each piece into a single node of a new, smaller graph.







Figure 1.11: Left: the six nodes colored by their refined piece, with every edge weight shown. Right: the same structure collapsed into two supernodes, X and Y, joined by one edge whose weight summarizes the total connection between the two original groups.




In the right panel of Figure 1.11, \(X\) and \(Y\) are supernodes. Each stands for a group of original nodes. The edge between them, with weight \(0.2\), summarizes the total connection between everything inside \(X\) and everything inside \(Y\). Internal edges become self connections on the supernodes, although those loops are omitted from the drawing. The membership of each supernode is also retained, so the final result can be mapped back to the original nodes.
This is the central mechanical trick behind Leiden. At the original level, the local moving step can only move one cell at a time. After refinement and aggregation, a single node in the new graph can represent an entire group of cells. The very same local-moving machinery, completely unchanged, can now move that whole group in one step, simply because it is now sitting behind one node instead of three. The coordinated three-node move that local moving could never find at the original level becomes an ordinary one-node move at the aggregated level.

title: 2  Leiden with R and Python
text:
ImportantDirect and package level interfaces



R’s igraph::cluster_leiden() and Python’s igraph.Graph.community_leiden() call the same underlying C library. Their main arguments and defaults match, except for automatic use of edge weights. R uses an edge attribute named weight when it is present. Python requires the attribute name or values to be passed through weights.
Python’s leidenalg.find_partition() is a separate interface. It takes a partition class and uses resolution_parameter rather than resolution. Scanpy 1.11.5 can use either leidenalg or igraph as its backend, so this chapter shows both Python interfaces.

title: 2  Leiden with R and Python
text:
2.2 Check agreement with ARI
The adjusted Rand index, or ARI, measures agreement between two groupings of the same observations. It compares whether pairs of observations are kept together or placed apart, then corrects for agreement expected by chance. An ARI of \(1\) means perfect agreement. A value near \(0\) means the agreement is close to chance. Group numbers do not need to match because ARI compares the grouping, not the labels assigned to it.

title: 2  Leiden with R and Python

We construct a nearest neighbour graph with \(k = 15\). Both examples use package functions for the neighbour search.

import igraph as ig
from sklearn.neighbors import kneighbors_graph

X = demo[["x", "y"]].to_numpy()

def knn_graph(X, k):
    adjacency = kneighbors_graph(X, n_neighbors=k, mode="connectivity")
    adjacency = adjacency.maximum(adjacency.T).astype("int64")
    return ig.Graph.Adjacency(adjacency, mode="undirected")

2.8 Add edge weights
makeKNNGraph() produces an unweighted graph. makeSNNGraph() builds a shared neighbour graph with Jaccard weights, as shown in Chapter 1 at Figure 1.6. The Python example uses a Gaussian weight based on distance. These are different weighting methods, but both show how weights can change a partition.

RPython


g_unw <- makeKNNGraph(X, k = 20)
g_w <- makeSNNGraph(X, k = 20, type = "jaccard")

set.seed(42)
p_unw <- cluster_leiden(g_unw, objective_function = "modularity",
                         resolution = 0.05, n_iterations = 2)
set.seed(42)
p_w <- cluster_leiden(g_w, objective_function = "modularity",
                       resolution = 0.05, n_iterations = 2)

cat("unweighted:", length(unique(membership(p_unw))), "clusters, ARI =",
    round(adjustedRandIndex(membership(p_unw), demo$true_community), 4), "\n")
cat("weighted (SNN):", length(unique(membership(p_w))), "clusters, ARI =",
    round(adjustedRandIndex(membership(p_w), demo$true_community), 4), "\n")
unweighted: 2 clusters, ARI = 0.3495
weighted (SNN): 3 clusters, ARI = 0.5835


def weighted_knn_graph(X, k):
    distances = kneighbors_graph(X, n_neighbors=k, mode="distance")
    sigma = np.median(distances.data)
    distances = distances.maximum(distances.T)
    distances.data = np.exp(-distances.data**2 / (2 * sigma**2))
    return ig.Graph.Weighted_Adjacency(distances, mode="undirected")

g_unw = knn_graph(X, 20)
g_w = weighted_knn_graph(X, 20)

p_unw = la.find_partition(g_unw, la.RBConfigurationVertexPartition,
                           resolution_parameter=0.1, seed=42)
p_w = la.find_partition(g_w, la.RBConfigurationVertexPartition,
                         resolution_parameter=0.1, weights="weight", seed=42)
print("unweighted:", len(set(p_unw.membership)), "clusters, ARI =",
      round(adjusted_rand_score(demo["true_community"], p_unw.membership), 4))
print("weighted:", len(set(p_w.membership)), "clusters, ARI =",
      round(adjusted_rand_score(demo["true_community"], p_w.membership), 4))

title: 2  Leiden with R and Python
text:
2.11 R interfaces
The direct function is igraph::cluster_leiden().
objective_function accepts "CPM" or "modularity". weights = NULL detects a weight attribute and weights = NA ignores it. resolution defaults to \(1\). beta controls randomness during refinement and defaults to \(0.01\). initial_membership supplies a starting partition. n_iterations controls the number of full passes and defaults to \(2\).
For reproducibility, call set.seed() before cluster_leiden(). The function uses R’s global random number generator.

2.11.1 Seurat
In Seurat, run FindNeighbors() and then FindClusters(algorithm = 4). Seurat expects coordinates stored in a dimensional reduction. Here the two simulated coordinates stand in for principal components. Chapter 4 applies the same interface after preprocessing gene expression data.
library(Seurat)

X_named <- X
rownames(X_named) <- demo$id
colnames(X_named) <- c("toy_1", "toy_2")

dummy_counts <- Matrix::Matrix(1, nrow = 3, ncol = nrow(X_named), sparse = TRUE,
                                dimnames = list(c("g1", "g2", "g3"), demo$id))
obj <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = dummy_counts)
obj[["toy"]] <- CreateDimReducObject(embeddings = X_named, key = "toy_",
                                      assay = DefaultAssay(obj))

obj <- FindNeighbors(obj, reduction = "toy", dims = 1:2, k.param = 15,
                     verbose = FALSE)
obj <- FindClusters(obj, algorithm = 4, resolution = 0.2,
                    random.seed = 42, verbose = FALSE)

length(unique(Idents(obj)))
adjustedRandIndex(Idents(obj), demo$true_community)
names(obj@graphs)
[1] 4
[1] 0.9022
[1] "RNA_nn" "RNA_snn"
algorithm = 4 selects Leiden. The default backend is leidenbase, which does not require Python. Setting leiden_method = "igraph" uses igraph::cluster_leiden() instead. With that backend, leiden_objective_function accepts "modularity" or "CPM".
FindNeighbors() stores a nearest neighbour graph as RNA_nn and a Jaccard weighted shared neighbour graph as RNA_snn. FindClusters() uses RNA_snn by default. Resolution \(0.2\) works better here than \(0.15\) because this is not the plain neighbour graph used earlier.

title: 2  Leiden with R and Python
text:
2.12 Python interfaces
The direct function is igraph.Graph.community_leiden(). Its objective, resolution, and beta arguments match the R function. Unlike R, Python does not select a weight edge attribute automatically.
leidenalg.find_partition() uses a partition class instead of an objective string. RBConfigurationVertexPartition provides modularity with a resolution parameter. CPMVertexPartition provides CPM. ModularityVertexPartition provides classic modularity without an adjustable resolution. The weights argument takes an attribute name or a list of values. n_iterations defaults to \(2\), while a negative value runs until a pass gives no improvement. seed controls reproducibility.

2.12.1 Scanpy
In Scanpy, run sc.pp.neighbors() and then sc.tl.leiden(). The simulated coordinates again stand in for principal components.
import anndata as ad
import scanpy as sc

adata = ad.AnnData(X=np.zeros((len(X), 3), dtype=np.float32))
adata.obs_names = demo["id"].astype(str)
adata.obsm["X_pca"] = X

sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_neighbors=15, use_rep="X_pca", random_state=0)
sc.tl.leiden(adata, resolution=0.05, key_added="leiden_0.05",
             random_state=0, flavor="igraph", n_iterations=2, directed=False)

adata.obs["leiden_0.05"].nunique()
adjusted_rand_score(demo["true_community"], adata.obs["leiden_0.05"])

sc.pp.neighbors() stores neighbour distances in adata.obsp["distances"] and a weighted symmetric graph in adata.obsp["connectivities"]. With the default method="umap", the connectivity calculation uses UMAP’s fuzzy graph construction. sc.tl.leiden() clusters the connectivity graph.






ImportantState the Scanpy backend explicitly



In Scanpy 1.11.5, sc.tl.leiden() defaults to flavor="leidenalg" and runs until convergence. The package warns that the backend will change to igraph. The example states flavor="igraph", n_iterations=2, and directed=False so its behavior is clear.
Both Scanpy backends use a modularity objective by default. The leidenalg backend selects RBConfigurationVertexPartition. The igraph backend sets objective_function="modularity". This differs from a direct call to igraph.Graph.community_leiden(), which defaults to CPM.

title: 2  Leiden with R and Python
text:
2.14 What clustering quality means
The word quality has two meanings here. The value returned by Leiden is optimization quality. It records how well a partition satisfies the selected objective. It does not show that the groups are correct or useful.
On these simulated data, ARI provides external quality because the true labels are known. Real data usually have no complete reference. Evaluation then combines several checks. Inspect whether conclusions persist across reasonable neighbour counts and resolutions. Repeat the fit across seeds. Look for very small or weakly separated clusters. In single cell data, also check whether clusters have coherent marker genes and whether they are driven by technical effects such as library size, batch, or poor quality cells.
A stable result can still reflect a poor graph or an unsuitable objective. A high objective value can also describe a partition that is unhelpful for the scientific question. Quality therefore needs evidence from the optimization, sensitivity checks, and the subject matter.

title: 2  Leiden with R and Python
text:
2.15 Summary
Leiden receives a graph, an objective, and a resolution. The neighbour count and weighting method define the graph. Resolution changes how that fixed graph is partitioned. Package defaults differ, so record these choices and check more than one reasonable setting. The exercise chapter applies this workflow to real single cell data, where the grouping is not known.

title: 1  Leiden clustering
text:
1.12 How refinement works
Refinement starts after local moving has stopped. Its input is the coarse partition produced by that step. In this example, the input contains one coarse parent community, \(\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\). Local moving could not improve it by moving one node at a time, but that does not mean its internal structure is good.
Leiden refines each coarse parent separately. Inside a parent, it creates a temporary partition in which every node starts as a singleton. A node may join another refined piece only when the move stays inside the same parent, passes the connection checks used by Leiden, and does not reduce the selected quality function at the chosen resolution. Among the acceptable moves, larger gains are preferred, with some randomness in the choice. Chapter 3 gives the exact calculation.







Figure 1.10: Refinement inside the coarse community ABCDEF. Leiden restarts from six singleton pieces, accepts moves supported by the strong triangle edges, rejects a move across the weak bridge, and returns ABC and DEF as two refined pieces.




Figure 1.10 shows one possible sequence.

Local moving supplies the coarse parent \(\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\). The dashed boundary records that all six nodes currently have the same coarse community label.
Refinement restarts the internal partition as \(A|B|C|D|E|F\). The parent boundary remains because every move is still restricted to this parent.
The strong edge between \(A\) and \(B\) supports a quality improving move, so they form the piece \(AB\). The same happens for \(D\) and \(E\), forming \(DE\). The accepted connections are green.
Node \(C\) has two strong connections to \(AB\), so joining that piece improves quality. Node \(F\) joins \(DE\) for the same reason. The temporary partition is now \(ABC|DEF\).
The only connection across the two pieces is the edge from \(C\) to \(D\) with weight \(0.20\). At the settings used for this example, crossing that bridge lowers quality, so the move is rejected.
Refinement returns \(\{A,B,C\}\) and \(\{D,E,F\}\). The blue and orange boundaries show the refined pieces.

The visiting order can change because refinement includes randomness. A different order might build the same pieces through a different sequence of accepted moves. The rules remain the same. Moves stay inside the coarse parent, must pass the connection checks, and cannot reduce quality.
The coarse partition and refined partition now serve different purposes. Refinement has not declared \(ABC\) and \(DEF\) to be final clusters. It has identified the units used to build the next graph. During aggregation, each refined piece becomes one node, while both nodes initially retain the community label of their shared coarse parent. The next local moving step can then reconsider either refined piece as a unit.

title: 3  How Leiden works mathematically
section: 3.17 Step 16: a bit more aggregate community labels
text:
3.17 Step 16: a bit more aggregate community labels
This point is easy to state and easy to misread, so it deserves its own step.
The aggregate graph’s nodes are defined by the refined partition, \(P_{\mathrm{refined}} = \{X, Y\}\) with \(X=\{A,B,C\}\) and \(Y=\{D,E,F\}\). But the initial community assignment on this new, smaller graph is not taken from the refined partition. It is taken from the original coarse partition, \(P = \{\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\}\), the one local moving actually produced.
Because \(P\) contained all six original nodes in a single community, both \(X\) and \(Y\) start out labelled as belonging to that same community on the aggregate graph, even though they are two distinct nodes of that graph.
\[X \neq Y \quad \text{as graph nodes,} \qquad c_X = c_Y \quad \text{as their starting community label.}\]
Refinement did not simply split the coarse community into its final answer. It created two separately movable units, \(X\) and \(Y\), while temporarily preserving the coarser grouping as their shared starting point for the next round of local moving. Whether that shared starting point survives depends on what local moving does next.

title: 3  How Leiden works mathematically
text:
4.2 Resolution
For CPM, merging pieces \(R\) and \(S\) raises the objective when
\[E(R,S) > \gamma\,|R||S|.\]
The connection between the pieces must exceed \(\gamma\) times the number of new pairs created by the merge. Raising \(\gamma\) therefore requires more edge weight.
For the final pieces \(ABC\) and \(DEF\), the only connecting edge has weight \(0.2\) and the size product is \(3\times3=9\). Their merger improves quality only when \(0.2 > 9\gamma\). At \(\gamma=0.24\), the right side is \(2.16\) and the pieces stay separate. At \(\gamma=0.02\), the right side is \(0.18\) and merging them raises the score. The threshold depends on both the connection weight and the sizes of the pieces.

title: 3  How Leiden works mathematically
text:
3.11 Step 10: the connection condition
A nonnegative gain is not the only requirement during refinement. Leiden first identifies singleton nodes that are sufficiently connected to their coarse parent. For each such node, it considers only destination pieces that are also sufficiently connected to that parent.
For a subset \(S\) inside a parent community \(C\), sufficient connection means
\[E\big(S,\ C\setminus S\big) \,\ge\, \gamma\,|S|\,|C\setminus S|.\]
Using \(R = C\setminus S\) in the merge formula from Step 9 gives this condition from \(\Delta Q(S, C\setminus S) \geq 0\). The connection from \(S\) to the rest of its parent must meet the threshold set by \(\gamma\) and the number of pairs involved.
Consider the move in which \(C\) joins the piece \(\{A,B\}\). The singleton \(C\) has total weight \(2.2\) to the other five nodes in its parent. Its condition is
\[2.2 \geq (0.24)(1)(5) = 1.2.\]
The destination \(\{A,B\}\) has total weight \(2\) to the other four nodes in the parent. Its condition is
\[2 \geq (0.24)(2)(4) = 1.92.\]
Both checks pass. The move also has the positive gain of \(1.52\) calculated in Step 9, so it is an acceptable refinement move. The conditions are checked before the move. The completed piece \(\{A,B,C\}\) is not required to pass the same check against \(\{D,E,F\}\) after the move.
After each Leiden iteration, every resulting community is connected and satisfies the stronger \(\gamma\) connection condition defined in the paper. Uniform density and subset optimality require repeated iterations. The connectivity guarantees section distinguishes these properties.

title: 3  How Leiden works mathematically
section: 3.17 Step 16: initial labels on the aggregate graph
text:
3.17 Step 16: initial labels on the aggregate graph
The aggregate graph’s nodes are defined by the refined partition, \(P_{\mathrm{refined}} = \{X, Y\}\) with \(X=\{A,B,C\}\) and \(Y=\{D,E,F\}\). But the initial community assignment on this new, smaller graph is not taken from the refined partition. It is taken from the original coarse partition, \(P = \{\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\}\), the one local moving actually produced.
Because \(P\) contained all six original nodes in a single community, both \(X\) and \(Y\) start out labelled as belonging to that same community on the aggregate graph, even though they are two distinct nodes of that graph.
\[X \neq Y \quad \text{as graph nodes,} \qquad c_X = c_Y \quad \text{as their starting community label.}\]
Refinement creates two movable units without making them final communities. Their shared coarse label provides the starting partition for the next local moving phase.

title: 3  How Leiden works mathematically
section: 3.8 Step 7: individual moves cannot split the coarse partition
text:
3.8 Step 7: individual moves cannot split the coarse partition
Apply the leaving formula to \(A\). Removing \(A\) from \(\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}\) leaves \(\{B,C,D,E,F\}\), a community of size \(5\).
\[\Delta Q_A = -w(A, \{B,C,D,E,F\}) + \gamma(6-1) = -(1+1) + (0.24)(5) = -2 + 1.2 = -0.8.\]
\(A\) has two edges of weight \(1\), so \(w(A,\text{rest}) = 2\). The move lowers quality by \(0.8\) and is rejected. By symmetry, the same calculation gives \(\Delta Q = -0.8\) for \(B\), \(E\), and \(F\).







Figure 3.4: Removing A from the coarse community lowers the objective from 2.6 to 1.8.




Now consider the boundary nodes \(C\) and \(D\), which touch the weak bridge.
\[\Delta Q_C = -w(C,\{A,B,D,E,F\}) + \gamma(5) = -(1+1+0.2) + 1.2 = -2.2+1.2 = -1.0.\]
\(C\) has edges to \(A\), \(B\), and \(D\), giving \(1+1+0.2=2.2\). Leaving lowers quality by \(1.0\), compared with \(0.8\) for \(A\). Both nodes receive the same reduction in the size penalty, but \(C\) would give up more internal edge weight. By symmetry, \(\Delta Q_D = -1.0\).
All six single node departures lower quality. The partition is therefore a local optimum with respect to individual node moves. It need not be the best partition overall.

title: 3  How Leiden works mathematically
text:
3.9 Step 8: comparing the two partitions
Compare the coarse partition against \(\{A,B,C\}, \{D,E,F\}\). Each triangle has internal edge weight \(e_C = 1+1+1=3\) and size \(n_C=3\), giving \(\binom{3}{2}=3\) pairs.
\[Q_{ABC} = 3 - (0.24)(3) = 3 - 0.72 = 2.28, \qquad Q_{DEF} = 2.28 \text{ by symmetry.}\]
\[Q_{\mathrm{refined}} = Q_{ABC} + Q_{DEF} = 2.28 + 2.28 = 4.56.\]







Figure 3.5: The partition {ABC},{DEF} scores 4.56 compared with 2.6 for the coarse partition.




Since \(4.56 > 2.6\), the partition into two triangles scores higher than the coarse partition. Step 7 showed why local moving cannot reach it from the chosen starting point. The improvement requires several nodes to change together.

title: 3  How Leiden works mathematically
text:
3.18 Step 17: moving refined pieces
At the original level, Step 7 showed that no individual node, \(A\) through \(F\), wanted to leave the coarse community on its own. Now run local moving again, on the aggregate graph, where \(X\) and \(Y\) are single nodes that happen to share a starting community label.
Local moving can now separate \(X\) from \(Y\) in one move. Before the move, both aggregate nodes share one community and the objective is \(Q_{\mathrm{coarse}} = 2.6\). After the move, they form separate communities and the objective is \(Q_{\mathrm{refined}} = 4.56\).
\[\Delta Q = Q_{\mathrm{refined}} - Q_{\mathrm{coarse}} = 4.56 - 2.6 = 1.96.\]
At the original level, local moving could move only one node at a time. On the aggregate graph, it can move a refined piece in one step.

title: 3  How Leiden works mathematically
text:
3.21 Step 20: algorithm summary







Figure 3.8: The complete Leiden procedure: local moving on the current graph until its queue is empty, refinement inside each resulting community, aggregation of the refined pieces into a smaller graph whose initial communities come from the coarse partition, repetition across levels, and a final flattening step back to the original nodes.




Figure 3.8 summarizes the sequence. Local moving stops when its queue is empty. Refinement finds smaller connected pieces inside each community. Aggregation turns those pieces into nodes while using the coarse partition for their starting labels. Local moving then runs on the aggregate graph. The levels end when every current node has its own community, and the labels are mapped back to the original observations.
